long_biography.plain_text:
Sir David Brown made motor racing central to Aston Martin's post-war revival. He recruited John Wyer to run the works team, stayed close to drivers and mechanics, and backed a sustained development programme. The effort culminated in 1959 with victory at the 24 Hours of Le Mans and the World Sports Car Championship.

Brown's involvement went beyond finance. An engineering apprentice who had built his own car and raced motorcycles in his youth, he brought practical mechanical judgement to the company. Aston Martin's team culture reflected that direct engagement: driver Roy Salvadori recalled an owner who shared the team's hotel, knew the mechanics by name and maintained friendships with his drivers.

review.notes: Owner-tag consolidation research context: [1] 24 Hours of Le Mans: Aston Martin's 1959 Le Mans victory under Brown's ownership was a defining achievement of his racing programme. [2] Aston Martin works racing team: The Aston Martin works team was the professional racing organisation Brown owned, financed and personally supported. [3] Automotive manufacturing: Brown used his family engineering group to own and develop Aston Martin, Lagonda and tractor manufacturing operations. [4] Brown industrial family: Brown belonged to the multigenerational family that founded, owned and successively led the Huddersfield engineering group. [5] David Brown Corporation: David Brown Corporation was the family engineering group Brown inherited operational responsibility for and expanded across multiple manufacturing sectors. [6] David Brown Tractors: David Brown Tractors was the agricultural-machinery operation Brown developed from the wider family engineering platform. [7] Export-led manufacturing expansion: International factories and export growth were defining components of Brown's expansion of the family manufacturing group. [8] Family ownership with professional management: Brown retained active family control while delegating authority to specialist managers, including John Wyer's leadership of Aston Martin's works team. [9] Industrial gear manufacturing: Industrial gear manufacture was the original and enduring technical base of the family company Brown expanded. [10] Industrialist: Brown actively expanded a family gear company into an international group spanning foundries, tractors, automobiles and shipbuilding. [11] Knighthood: Brown was appointed a Knight Bachelor in 1968 for services to export. [12] Lagonda: Brown acquired Lagonda in 1947 and used its engine technology in the post-war Aston Martin DB cars. [13] Le Mans-winning team owner: Brown owned Aston Martin when its works team won the 1959 24 Hours of Le Mans. [14] Luxury car manufacturing: Aston Martin's DB sports and grand-touring cars became Brown's defining luxury-manufacturing legacy. [15] Metal casting: Brown expanded the family engineering group into foundries and industrial castings as part of its manufacturing diversification. [16] Post-founder succession governance: Brown succeeded his father in the engineering company founded by his grandfather and became its active chairman and expansion leader. [17] Sports car racing: Sports-car endurance racing was the specific discipline in which Brown's Aston Martin works programme achieved its defining success. [18] Tractor manufacturing: Brown expanded the group into tractor manufacturing and developed the David Brown tractor line after its Ferguson relationship. [19] Vertical integration: Brown combined group engineering capacity with the acquired Aston Martin chassis and Lagonda engine and expanded control of industrial production capabilities. [20] World Sportscar Championship: Brown's Aston Martin programme won the 1959 World Sportscar Championship alongside its Le Mans success.
